disclaimer: PeptideX is an educational resource about peptide science. It is not medical advice and does not diagnose, treat, or recommend any substance for any person. It provides no dosing information and does not help anyone obtain any drug or research chemical. Talk to a qualified clinician about any health decision.

studies.results_summary: Researchers reported more cell migration and survival under stress, linked to FAK-paxillin signaling.
studies.limitations: Cell study only. The mechanism has not been shown in people.

studies.population: Cell cultures, chick membrane preparations and rats
studies.intervention_identity: BPC-157 in laboratory and animal models
studies.results_summary: Researchers reported new blood-vessel formation linked to VEGFR2 signaling and the nitric-oxide system.
studies.limitations: Laboratory and animal findings only; not shown in people.

studies.population: The published musculoskeletal literature on BPC-157
studies.intervention_identity: BPC-157 (as studied across the reviewed literature)
studies.results_summary: The review counted 36 studies of BPC-157 in musculoskeletal research, of which 35 were preclinical and 1 was clinical.
studies.limitations: A count of study designs is not a finding of benefit; the underlying literature is mostly preclinical and much of it comes from a single research group.

studies.population: All human evidence on BPC-157 located by the review
studies.intervention_identity: BPC-157 (as reported in the three underlying human reports)
studies.results_summary: The review found 3 human studies (30 people in total): a retrospective chart review with phone follow-up of 16 patients with knee pain at one clinic (no control group, no validated outcome measures; some also received another peptide), a 12-person retrospective report in interstitial cystitis, and a two-person pilot measuring blood tests at one clinic, all three from the same clinician. It rated them poor quality and the overall certainty of evidence very low.
studies.limitations: The underlying reports lacked control groups and validated measures and were small.

studies.population: Mice and cell systems in the first description of MOTS-c
studies.intervention_identity: MOTS-c in cell and mouse models
outcomes_studied: folate cycle and purine synthesis pathways
studies.results_summary: Researchers reported that MOTS-c acts mainly on skeletal muscle in mice and affects the folate cycle and purine synthesis, leading to activation of the enzyme AMPK.
studies.limitations: Mouse and cell findings only. FDA's evaluation notes that the molecular target through which MOTS-c acts remains unknown. Not shown in people.
studies.funding_conflicts: Some researchers on the early MOTS-c studies disclosed financial ties to a company developing related compounds.

studies.population: Mice of different ages; human measurements of the body's own MOTS-c around exercise
studies.intervention_identity: MOTS-c in mouse models; measurement of endogenous MOTS-c in people
outcomes_studied: the body's own MOTS-c levels in muscle and blood around exercise
studies.results_summary: Mouse studies reported effects on diet-related and age-related metabolic changes and on physical performance in young, middle-aged and old mice. A human component reported exercise-related increases in the body's own MOTS-c in muscle and blood.
studies.limitations: The human component measured the MOTS-c the body makes itself; it does not establish the effects or safety of MOTS-c given as a preparation. Mouse findings may not apply to people.
studies.funding_conflicts: Some researchers on the early MOTS-c studies disclosed financial ties to a company developing related compounds.

studies.intervention_identity: No substance administered; measurement of the body's own MOTS-c
outcomes_studied: the body's own MOTS-c levels after endurance exercise
link between MOTS-c levels and fitness
studies.results_summary: The study found only a non-significant trend in the body's own MOTS-c after endurance exercise and no link to fitness.
studies.limitations: Observational measurement of naturally occurring MOTS-c; it cannot show cause and effect and says nothing about administered MOTS-c.

studies.population: Human plasma samples in the first description of GHK
studies.intervention_identity: Identification of the GHK peptide in human plasma
outcomes_studied: presence and identity of the peptide
studies.results_summary: First description of the three-amino-acid peptide glycyl-L-histidyl-L-lysine (GHK) in human plasma in the 1970s.
studies.limitations: An identification study; it is not evidence of any clinical effect.

outcomes_studied: collagen production by fibroblasts in culture
studies.results_summary: The study reported increased collagen production by fibroblasts in culture. Early cell studies also proposed that GHK-Cu acts as a carrier that moves copper into cells.
studies.limitations: Cell-culture findings do not establish clinical effects in people, and these effects have not been established in human tissue.

studies.population: Patients with venous stasis ulcers; 86 evaluable patients
studies.results_summary: A randomized, evaluator-blinded trial: the tripeptide-copper cream performed no better than placebo.
studies.limitations: A single older trial in one ulcer type; a null result for this formulation and population.

studies.population: Patients with diabetic foot ulcers at multiple centers, all also receiving standardized wound care
studies.intervention_identity: GHK-Cu gel applied to skin, plus standardized wound care
studies.comparator: Vehicle gel, plus standardized wound care
studies.results_summary: A multicenter randomized, evaluator-blinded, placebo-controlled trial: ulcer area closed faster with the gel than with the vehicle gel. That is a measure of area change, not the share of patients healed.
studies.limitations: The trial was never replicated, and the product never became an approved drug.

studies.population: People recovering after laser skin resurfacing; 13 people completed
studies.intervention_identity: GHK-Cu skin products applied to skin after laser resurfacing
studies.results_summary: A randomized trial: blinded and computer assessments found no differences in redness, wrinkles or overall skin quality. Participants using the GHK-Cu products reported higher satisfaction.
studies.limitations: Very small sample (13 people completed); satisfaction was self-reported while the blinded assessments were null.

peptides.what_it_is: A synthetic 15-amino-acid peptide derived from a protein described in human gastric juice. It has been studied mainly in laboratory and animal models of tissue injury. Much of the animal literature comes from a single research group, so independent replication is limited.
peptides.molecular_identity: A synthetic 15-amino-acid peptide; a partial sequence of the larger body protection compound protein described in human gastric juice.
not_to_be_confused_with: The larger body protection compound protein described in gastric juice (BPC-157 is a 15-amino-acid partial sequence of it)
Different salt forms, which regulators treat as different substances
Combination products with other peptides, which are a different thing
peptides.formulation_route_distinctions: Different salt forms are treated as different substances by regulators. Combination products with other peptides are not the same as BPC-157 alone.

mechanism.text: Proposed, from lab and animal studies only: in rat tendon cells, researchers reported more cell migration and survival under stress, linked to FAK-paxillin signaling. In cell, chick-membrane and rat studies, they reported new blood-vessel formation linked to VEGFR2 signaling and the nitric-oxide system. These mechanisms have not been shown in people.

peptides.safety_summary: No clinical safety data in humans were located in the sources searched through 2026-11-17. FDA states that compounded drugs containing BPC-157 may pose immunogenicity and impurity risks and that the agency lacks sufficient information to know whether the drug would cause harm when administered to humans. The identity and purity of products labeled for research use are not established.
peptides.evidence_limitations: The systematic reviews cited in this dataset located no controlled human data and no clinical safety data in humans. Animal findings may not apply to people. The human reports lacked control groups and validated measures, and were small.

evidence_stage.human: Three small uncontrolled reports; no published randomized controlled trial was found in the literature searched through 2026-11-17.
evidence_stage.limits: The systematic reviews cited in this dataset located no controlled human data and no clinical safety data in humans. Animal findings may not apply to people. The human reports lacked control groups and validated measures, and were small.

studied: Cell and animal studies, mostly in rats, of tendon, muscle, ligament, bone and gut injury models. A 2025 systematic review of the musculoskeletal literature counted 36 studies, of which 35 were preclinical and 1 was clinical.

Human reports are few and small: a retrospective chart review with phone follow-up of 16 patients with knee pain at one clinic (no control group, no validated outcome measures; some also received another peptide), a 12-person retrospective report in interstitial cystitis (a bladder pain condition), and a two-person pilot measuring blood tests at one clinic, all three from the same clinician. A 2026 systematic review of all human evidence found these 3 studies (30 people in total), rated them poor quality, and rated the overall certainty of evidence very low.
Small registered studies exist. A trial registration is not evidence that a substance works, and no registered trial had reported results in the sources searched through 2026-11-17.
not_established: Effectiveness for any condition in people
Whether lab or animal mechanisms apply in humans
The identity and purity of products labeled for research use

peptides.what_it_is: A synthetic seven-amino-acid fragment of thymosin beta-4, a 43-amino-acid protein. TB-500 is a common name, not a USAN (United States Adopted Name), and multiple salts and derivatives are sold under the name. FDA states that TB-500 and thymosin beta-4 are not the same substance.
peptides.molecular_identity: A synthetic seven-amino-acid fragment of the 43-amino-acid protein thymosin beta-4. The name does not map reliably to one molecule in commerce: multiple salts and derivatives are sold under it.
not_to_be_confused_with: Full-length thymosin beta-4, the 43-amino-acid protein (a different substance; the human trials in this area tested the full-length protein)
The non-acetylated form used in the fragment's animal studies, whose profile FDA says cannot be extrapolated to TB-500
Other salts and derivatives sold under the same common name
peptides.formulation_route_distinctions: Fragment versus full-length protein is the central distinction: most of the evidence in this area concerns the full-length protein, not the fragment. Salt and derivative forms sold under the name also differ from one another.

mechanism.text: No mechanism has been established for TB-500 itself. Claims made for the fragment borrow from research on full-length thymosin beta-4, a different substance. The one direct in-vitro test of TB-500 itself located in FDA's evaluation did not outperform control.

peptides.safety_summary: FDA's evaluation of TB-500 bulk substances (May 2026) documents safety concerns for specified peptide substances and routes. FDA found no information in the medical literature where TB-500 itself was administered to patients for any condition, so there is no human safety record for the fragment itself. The identity of products sold under the name varies, because multiple salts and derivatives are sold under it.
peptides.evidence_limitations: Most evidence in this area concerns full-length thymosin beta-4, a different substance. The fragment's animal data used a different (non-acetylated) form whose profile FDA says cannot be extrapolated to TB-500. There are no human administration studies of the fragment itself in the sources searched through 2026-11-17.

evidence_stage.lab: One direct in-vitro test of TB-500 itself did not outperform control (per FDA's evaluation).
evidence_stage.animal: Animal data exist for a different (non-acetylated) form; FDA states its profile cannot be extrapolated to TB-500.
evidence_stage.human: None. FDA found no published study in which TB-500 itself was administered to patients for any condition (sources searched through 2026-11-17).
evidence_stage.limits: Most evidence in this area concerns full-length thymosin beta-4, a different substance, and cannot be read as evidence about the fragment.

studied: FDA's evaluation records that the human trials in this area tested full-length thymosin beta-4, not TB-500.
The fragment's animal data used a non-acetylated form whose profile FDA says cannot be extrapolated to TB-500.
The one direct in-vitro test of TB-500 itself located in FDA's evaluation did not outperform control.
not_established: Any effect of TB-500 itself in people (it has never been administered to patients in any published study located)
Safety of TB-500 itself in people
Equivalence between TB-500 and full-length thymosin beta-4 (FDA states they are not the same substance)
The identity of any specific product sold under the name

peptides.what_it_is: A small three-amino-acid peptide (glycine-histidine-lysine) that binds copper. It was first described in human plasma in the 1970s. It is sold as an ingredient in skin-care cosmetics; it is not an approved drug ingredient.
peptides.molecular_identity: The tripeptide glycyl-L-histidyl-L-lysine bound to copper(II).
not_to_be_confused_with: GHK without copper (the free tripeptide), a different substance; studies of one do not automatically describe the other
Other copper peptides with different amino-acid sequences
Skin-applied cosmetic products versus injectable preparations: every published human study used skin-applied formulations, and FDA's listed concern applies to injectable routes
peptides.formulation_route_distinctions: Every published human study used skin-applied (topical) formulations. FDA's compounding position distinguishes routes: GHK-Cu except for injectable routes sits in Category 1 of the 503A nominations (under evaluation), while the injectable form's nomination was withdrawn.

mechanism.text: Proposed, from cell-culture studies: early cell studies proposed that it acts as a carrier that moves copper into cells, and a 1988 study reported increased collagen production by fibroblasts in culture. Cell-culture findings do not establish clinical effects in people, and these effects have not been established in human tissue.

peptides.safety_summary: The human record is topical only: three small randomized trials from 1992-2006 with mixed results. No published human trial of GHK-Cu given by injection was found in the sources searched through 2026-11-17, and FDA noted possible immunogenicity and impurity concerns and limited human data for compounded injectables. Cosmetic availability is not drug evidence: cosmetics do not undergo FDA premarket approval.
peptides.evidence_limitations: The human trials are old, small, and mixed; the one positive result was never replicated. Much of the review literature comes from the peptide's discoverer and colleagues; the discoverer founded a company selling copper-peptide products, a conflict of interest readers should know about. The three trials in this dataset are the independent human record.

evidence_stage.human: Topical only: the randomized human studies located by the stated search are three small topical trials from 1992-2006 with mixed results. No published human trial of GHK-Cu given by injection was found in the sources searched through 2026-11-17.
evidence_stage.limits: The human trials are old, small, and mixed; the one positive result was never replicated. Cosmetic availability is not drug evidence.

studied: Cell-culture studies of cell growth, copper uptake and collagen production, and rodent wound studies: laboratory and animal work only.
A 1992 randomized, evaluator-blinded trial in venous stasis ulcers (86 evaluable patients): a tripeptide-copper cream performed no better than placebo.

A 1994 multicenter randomized, evaluator-blinded, placebo-controlled trial of a GHK-Cu gel in diabetic foot ulcers, with all patients also receiving standardized wound care: ulcer area closed faster with the gel than with the vehicle gel. That is a measure of area change, not the share of patients healed; the trial was never replicated, and the product never became an approved drug.

A 2006 randomized trial after laser skin resurfacing (13 people completed): blinded and computer assessments found no differences in redness, wrinkles or overall skin quality. Participants using the GHK-Cu products reported higher satisfaction.

Much of the review literature comes from the peptide's discoverer and colleagues; the discoverer founded a company selling copper-peptide products, a conflict of interest readers should know about. The three trials above are the independent human record.
not_established: Any benefit beyond the mixed topical record described in this card
Any effect or safety of injected GHK-Cu in people

aliases: Mitochondrial open reading frame of the 12S rRNA-c
peptides.what_it_is: A 16-amino-acid peptide encoded in mitochondrial DNA rather than nuclear DNA. It was first described in 2015 and is studied as a possible signaling molecule in metabolism. It is a research compound, not a medicine.
peptides.molecular_identity: A 16-amino-acid peptide encoded by an open reading frame in the mitochondrial 12S rRNA region of mitochondrial DNA.
not_to_be_confused_with: The MOTS-c the body makes itself (measured in blood or muscle) versus MOTS-c given as a substance: different questions, different evidence
CB4211, a chemically modified analogue developed from MOTS-c, which is a separate molecule; its results are not MOTS-c results
Different salt forms, which regulators treat as different substances
peptides.formulation_route_distinctions: Measurements of the body's own MOTS-c do not establish the effects or safety of an administered preparation. An analogue's results are not MOTS-c results. Different salt forms are treated as different substances by regulators.

mechanism.text: Proposed, from mouse and cell studies: researchers reported that it acts mainly on skeletal muscle in mice and affects the folate cycle and purine synthesis, leading to activation of the enzyme AMPK. FDA's evaluation notes that the molecular target through which MOTS-c acts remains unknown. These mechanisms have not been shown in people.

peptides.safety_summary: There is no human safety record for MOTS-c given as a substance: FDA's May 2026 evaluation did not identify clinical studies evaluating administration of MOTS-c in human subjects and had not identified any human exposure data for drug products containing MOTS-c by any route. What a person's own blood level of MOTS-c means for their health is not established.
peptides.evidence_limitations: Mouse findings may not apply to people. Observational human data cannot show cause and effect, and the human data measure the body's own MOTS-c, not an administered preparation.

evidence_stage.human: Observational measurements of naturally occurring MOTS-c only; no completed human study of MOTS-c given as a substance was identified in the sources searched through 2026-11-17.
evidence_stage.limits: Mouse findings may not apply to people. Observational human data cannot show cause and effect.

studied: Mouse studies of diet-related and age-related metabolic changes and of physical performance in young, middle-aged and old mice. Findings were reported in mice only.

Human studies that measured the body's own MOTS-c levels, for example before and after exercise. Results are mixed: one study reported exercise-related increases in muscle and blood, and another (30 adults) found only a non-significant trend after endurance exercise and no link to fitness. These are measurements of the MOTS-c the body makes itself; they do not establish the effects or safety of MOTS-c given as a preparation.
Some researchers on the early studies disclosed financial ties to a company developing related compounds.
not_established: Any effect of MOTS-c given to people
Whether mouse findings carry over to humans
What a person's blood level of MOTS-c means for their health

explainers.title: What is a peptide?
explainers.summary: A peptide is a short chain of amino acids — a small, precise message molecule the body makes and uses constantly.
explainers.body:
A peptide is a short chain of amino acids — the same building blocks that make up proteins. If a protein is a long paragraph, a peptide is a short phrase: typically a few to a few dozen amino acids linked in a specific order. The order is the whole point. Change one link in the chain and the message the molecule carries changes with it.

The body makes thousands of peptides on its own. Many act as messengers: released in one place, they travel to cells elsewhere and instruct them — release another substance, grow, repair, stand down. Others are fragments of ordinary proteins, including the pieces digestion creates from the protein in food.

Scientists study peptides because they are precise. A peptide usually fits one kind of receptor — a docking site on a cell — the way a key fits one lock, so its signal is specific rather than broad. That precision comes with fragility: the body is full of enzymes whose job is to dismantle peptides, and most are broken down within minutes. Peptides are, by design, temporary signals.

This is general education only. For any question about your own health, talk to a qualified clinician.
explainers.sources_note: Based on standard biochemistry references (e.g., Lehninger Principles of Biochemistry) and National Institutes of Health educational resources.

explainers.title: How peptides work as signals in the body
explainers.summary: Signaling peptides bind to specific receptors on cells, triggering brief, amplified cascades — pulses, not permanent states.
explainers.body:
Cells coordinate chemically, and peptides are one of the body's main messaging systems. A signaling peptide is released by one cell, drifts through the fluid around cells or rides the bloodstream, and binds to a receptor — a docking site on a target cell shaped for that particular signal.

Binding switches the receptor on. The receptor triggers a cascade inside the cell, and the cell changes its behavior: it may release signals of its own, take up nutrients, divide, or quiet down. Three features of this system matter for understanding the science.

First, specificity: a signal fits its own receptor, not others, so messages are addressed rather than broadcast. Second, amplification: one binding event can set off a chain that affects many molecules, so a tiny amount of signal can have a large — but still controlled — effect. Third, brevity: enzymes dismantle signaling peptides quickly, so signals arrive as pulses. The body turns them off as deliberately as it turns them on.

Researchers study these pathways first to understand normal physiology. Most published work is about how the system operates, not about intervening in it.

This is general education only. For any question about your own health, talk to a qualified clinician.
explainers.sources_note: Based on standard cell-biology and biochemistry textbook accounts of peptide signaling and receptor function.

explainers.title: Peptides in everyday science
explainers.summary: Peptides appear wherever proteins do — digestion, skin biology, nature's defenses, food science — each field with its own evidence standards.
explainers.body:
Peptides are not exotic laboratory inventions. They show up wherever proteins do, and several ordinary fields of science work with them every day.

Digestion is the most familiar example: breaking down the protein in food produces peptides, some of which the gut absorbs, and researchers study the roles such fragments play in normal physiology. Skin biology involves peptide signals that help coordinate the renewal and maintenance of tissue, an active area of dermatology and materials research. In nature, many organisms produce peptides as part of their defenses, and scientists study those molecules to understand how they interact with microbes under laboratory conditions. Food science and agriculture also work with peptides, as ingredients and as objects of study.

One caution ties these fields together: the word "peptide" on a label names a category of molecule, not a promise of any effect. What matters is the specific evidence for a specific use — which is exactly what the reading-research explainers in this library are for.

This is general education only. For any question about your own health, talk to a qualified clinician.
explainers.sources_note: Based on standard biochemistry references and National Institutes of Health educational resources on proteins and digestion.

explainers.title: How peptides are made in a lab
explainers.summary: Research peptides are usually built one amino acid at a time by automated machines — and making the molecule is the easy part of the science.
explainers.body:
Most research peptides are built rather than harvested. The standard approach, developed in the second half of the twentieth century and now heavily automated, assembles a peptide one amino acid at a time on a tiny solid support: each building block is added in the intended sequence, the growing chain stays anchored while it is built, and at the end the finished chain is released and cleaned up for use in experiments.

Automation changed the field. A machine can produce a short, precise sequence quickly, so a laboratory can obtain exactly the molecule it wants to study. Longer and more complex chains are a different story: they can fold wrongly, clump together, or break, and the yield of usable material falls as length grows. Living cells are also used to produce some larger peptide and protein molecules, by giving them the genetic instructions — a different route with its own complications.

However a peptide is made, making it is the easy part of the science. The hard part is everything that comes after: showing what it does, in what system, how reliably — and whether any of it survives the move from a dish to a living body.

This is general education only. For any question about your own health, talk to a qualified clinician.
explainers.sources_note: Based on standard biochemistry and peptide-chemistry textbook accounts of solid-phase peptide synthesis.

explainers.title: Why peptides are hard to study
explainers.summary: The body dismantles peptides within minutes, so stability and delivery are the field's central unsolved scientific problems.
explainers.body:
Peptides are, by design, temporary. The body treats loose peptides as material to recycle: enzymes in the gut, the blood, and tissues cut them apart, and the kidneys clear the pieces. A peptide that performs beautifully in a dish may last only minutes inside a living system.

That creates the field's central scientific problem: stability. Researchers study how a sequence might resist breakdown for longer, and how a fragile molecule could reach its intended target intact at all — a delivery problem that remains unsolved for most peptides. It also creates a measurement problem. Experiments in a dish can hold a peptide at concentrations, and for durations, that a body would never sustain, so dish results can look far stronger than anything physiology would allow.

This is why peptide papers so often end with the same honest sentence in different words: promising in the model, unproven beyond it. The distance between those two statements is most of what peptide science is working on.

This is general education only. For any question about your own health, talk to a qualified clinician.
explainers.sources_note: Based on standard pharmacology and biochemistry textbook accounts of peptide stability and metabolism.

explainers.title: From lab bench to approved medicine: the long road
explainers.summary: Discovery becomes an approved medicine through staged testing over a decade or more — and most candidates fail along the way, by design.
explainers.body:
A discovery becomes an approved medicine through a staged process built to answer three questions in order: is it safe enough to test in people, does it do anything measurable, and does that benefit outweigh its risks in real patients?

The stages run from basic research — what the molecule is and what it does in dishes and animals — into phased human trials: small safety studies first, then larger studies looking for an effect, then large confirmatory trials. After that, a regulator reviews the complete body of data, not the headlines, and decides whether the evidence supports approval for a specific use.

Most candidates fail somewhere along this road. That is the system working as intended, not malfunctioning: the gauntlet exists precisely because early promise is common and real benefit is rare. The journey commonly takes a decade or more, which is why "being studied" and "approved" are separated by years of evidence rather than by an announcement.

Anything that has not completed this road may be interesting science. It is not an approved medicine, and no label wording changes that.

This is general education only. For any question about your own health, talk to a qualified clinician.
explainers.sources_note: Based on U.S. Food and Drug Administration educational materials on the drug development and approval process.

explainers.title: Categories of peptides researchers study
explainers.summary: Peptide research is organized by field — signaling, antimicrobial, structural, and others — and a category being studied says nothing about any product.
explainers.body:
Researchers organize peptide research by the questions being asked, not by products. A few of the main fields:

Signaling peptides are the molecules cells use to coordinate with one another. Researchers are studying how these pathways work in areas such as metabolism, growth, and repair — mostly basic physiology, in cells and animals.

Antimicrobial peptides are molecules many organisms produce as part of their natural defenses. Researchers are studying how they interact with microbes in laboratory settings, and what those interactions reveal about immunity in general.

Structural peptides are studied for the shapes they form and the materials those shapes can create — a field that belongs as much to materials science as to biology.

Other active areas include peptides in neuroscience, skin biology, and agriculture. Two cautions apply to all of them. A category being studied describes a research question, not a treatment. And in every one of these fields, most of the work is early-stage — the distance from a research category to anything a person could use is the full length of the road described in the explainer on how medicines get approved.

This is general education only. For any question about your own health, talk to a qualified clinician.
explainers.sources_note: Based on standard biochemistry references and National Institutes of Health research overviews.

explainers.title: Animal studies vs human studies: why the gap matters
explainers.summary: A result in a mouse is a result in a mouse — animal work is essential and preclinical, and it cannot substitute for human trials.
explainers.body:
A result in a mouse is a result in a mouse. Animal studies are essential science: they reveal mechanisms, flag dangers early, and decide what is worth the cost and risk of testing in people. What they cannot do is substitute for human evidence.

Species differ in exactly the ways that matter here. Metabolism differs — a peptide dismantled in minutes by human enzymes may circulate far longer in a rodent. Receptors differ, lifespans differ, and the diseases researchers model in animals are simplified versions of human conditions. Amounts used in animal work are also scaled in ways that do not translate directly to people.

This is why regulators require phased human trials, and why careful scientists describe animal findings as "preclinical": before the clinic, not instead of it. When a headline converts a rodent result into a human promise, it has skipped the very step where most candidates fail — and it has usually skipped it on purpose, because the honest version is less exciting.

This is general education only. For any question about your own health, talk to a qualified clinician.
explainers.sources_note: Based on National Institutes of Health guidance on preclinical research and the translation of animal findings.

explainers.title: How to read a peptide study critically
explainers.summary: Five checks — system, sample size, controls, what was measured, and who paid — separate a finding worth taking seriously from a headline.
explainers.body:
Five checks, in order, will carry you through most research claims.

First: what system? A dish, an animal, or people. Each answers a different question, and only the last one is about human beings.

Second: how many? Tiny samples produce dramatic-looking results by chance. Look for the number of subjects and whether the study was large enough to detect what it claims.

Third: compared to what? Without a control group — and ideally blinding, so neither the subjects nor the people measuring know who received what — apparent improvement may be expectation, the passage of time, or noise.

Fourth: what was actually measured? A laboratory marker moving is not the same as a health outcome improving. Results built on substitute measures, presented as if they were outcomes, deserve special skepticism.

Fifth: who paid, and where was it published? Funding does not invalidate work, but it is context. And a peer-reviewed journal has had independent experts check the paper; a preprint has not had that check yet.

A study that survives all five checks is worth taking seriously — as one study. What a body of evidence says is a separate question, covered in the explainer on systematic reviews.

This is general education only. For any question about your own health, talk to a qualified clinician.
explainers.sources_note: Based on National Institutes of Health and National Library of Medicine guidance on evaluating health research.

explainers.title: Red flags in peptide headlines
explainers.summary: "Breakthrough" language, before-and-after imagery, unnamed sources, and urgency are marketing tells — here is how to spot them.
explainers.body:
Certain phrases and devices should slow you down whenever health research is being sold to you.

"Breakthrough" and "miracle." Reporting that sounds like advertising usually is advertising.

Before-and-after imagery. It shows two photographs, not a controlled comparison. It is a marketing device, not evidence — and its presence is itself information about the seller.

"Clinically studied," with no citation. Studied is not shown. The study may be in animals, tiny, unpublished, or about a different molecule entirely.

A single dramatic percentage with no sample size attached. Real findings come with numbers of subjects and measures of uncertainty.

Testimonials in place of data, and urgency — limited offers, expiring discounts — attached to anything health-related.

And the quietest red flag: a claim that names no checkable source. Reputable research can always be traced to a paper, a trial-registry entry, or a regulator's record. A headline that cannot survive the five checks in "How to read a peptide study critically" is a sales pitch wearing a lab coat.

This is general education only. For any question about your own health, talk to a qualified clinician.
explainers.sources_note: Based on National Library of Medicine and U.S. Food and Drug Administration guidance on health claims and misleading marketing.

explainers.title: What a systematic review is, and why one study is rarely the answer
explainers.summary: Systematic reviews gather and grade every study on a question — the strongest summary of evidence, and the antidote to cherry-picked single papers.
explainers.body:
Single studies disagree. They use different samples, different methods, and different luck — so a literature can contain one paper showing a striking effect and several quieter ones showing none.

A systematic review is the antidote. Researchers define, in advance, a precise question and the rules for finding every study that bears on it. They then gather those studies, grade their quality, and summarize what the whole body of evidence says. Its stricter cousin, the meta-analysis, also pools the numbers statistically. Done well, this is the strongest form of evidence summary there is, because it shows the entire landscape — including the null results and failures that never became headlines.

Done badly, it averages strong and weak studies into false confidence, which is why good reviews grade study quality instead of treating every paper as equal.

The practical lesson is simple: trust bodies of evidence over single papers. Any claim resting on one small study — however exciting — is a preliminary sketch, not a conclusion.

This is general education only. For any question about your own health, talk to a qualified clinician.
explainers.sources_note: Based on National Library of Medicine guidance on systematic reviews and evidence synthesis.

explainers.title: What FDA approval means — and what it doesn't
explainers.summary: Approval is specific: one product, one use, one population, judged on full trial data — and it never transfers to other products or uses.
explainers.body:
In the United States, FDA approval means that a specific product, manufactured to a defined standard, has been shown — in adequate, well-controlled trials — to be safe and effective for a specific use, in a specific population, and that its benefits for that use outweigh its known risks.

Every qualifier in that sentence carries weight. Approval is not a judgment that a molecule is "good." It does not transfer to other uses, other populations, or other products made from similar ingredients. And it is not necessarily permanent: regulators can and do revise or withdraw approvals as new evidence accumulates.

Approval also says nothing about substances that have never been through the process. A published paper is not an approval. A patent is not an approval. A citation count is not an approval. A label reading "research use only" is not an approval. And a product being sold is not evidence that it was ever reviewed.

The regulator keeps public records of what is actually approved. That record — not marketing language — is the ground truth.

This is general education only. For any question about your own health, talk to a qualified clinician.
explainers.sources_note: Based on U.S. Food and Drug Administration educational materials on drug approval.

explainers.title: What "research use only" actually means
explainers.summary: The label marks laboratory materials, full stop — it is not a loophole for human use and implies no pharmaceutical testing or standards.
explainers.body:
"Research use only" is a regulatory label for materials supplied for laboratory work: experiments in dishes, instruments, and controlled research settings. It marks the boundary of what the material was made and sold for.

It is not a loophole. The label does not create a legal category of human use. It does not imply the material was manufactured to pharmaceutical standards. And it does not come with the testing — for identity, purity, sterility, or effect — that approved medicines are required to undergo. Materials under this label have not been evaluated by regulators for use in people.

That is why the label matters when marketing points the other way. When a seller pairs "research use only" with imagery or testimonials suggesting personal use, the label and the marketing contradict each other — and the label is the legally meaningful part.

In short: research use only means research use only.

This is general education only. For any question about your own health, talk to a qualified clinician.
explainers.sources_note: Based on U.S. Food and Drug Administration guidance on research-use-only labeling.

terms.plain_language: FDA approval is a U.S. regulator's decision that a specific product, manufactured to a defined standard, has been shown in adequate clinical trials to be safe and effective for a specific use, with its benefits outweighing its known risks for that use.
terms.does_not_mean: It does not mean a substance or ingredient is approved in general, for other uses, or in other products — and approval is never conferred by a published paper, a patent, a citation count, or the fact that something is being sold.

terms.plain_language: A label for materials supplied solely for laboratory research. It defines the legal purpose of the material: experiments in controlled research settings, not use in or on people.
terms.does_not_mean: It is not a loophole for human use, not a quality grade, and not evidence that the material was made or tested to pharmaceutical standards.

terms.plain_language: A legal category for medicines that may be supplied to a patient only under a clinician's prescription, because using them safely requires professional judgment and monitoring.
terms.does_not_mean: It does not mean the medicine is stronger, better, or more desirable than a non-prescription option. The category describes a legal safeguard, not a ranking of quality or power.

terms.plain_language: Off-label use is when a clinician prescribes an approved medicine for a use, population, or form that the regulator did not approve. The practice is legal and sometimes supported by evidence, but that particular use has not itself passed the approval process.
terms.does_not_mean: It does not mean the use is approved, endorsed by the regulator, or backed by the same level of trial evidence as the approved use.

terms.plain_language: The staged testing of a candidate medicine in people. Phase 1 checks basic safety in a small group. Phase 2 explores whether the candidate shows an effect, and at what cost in side effects. Phase 3 confirms benefit and risk in a large group. Only after these stages can a regulator consider approval.
terms.does_not_mean: Being "in trials" — even in Phase 3 — does not mean a product works or will be approved. Most candidates fail somewhere along the way.

terms.plain_language: The process in which independent experts in the same field examine a study before a journal publishes it, checking its methods, analysis, and whether its conclusions follow from its data. It is a quality filter.
terms.does_not_mean: It does not mean the findings are proven true. Peer-reviewed papers can be wrong and are sometimes retracted — and work that has not been through review at all, such as a preprint, has not yet had even that check.

terms.plain_language: A complete study manuscript posted publicly before peer review, so other researchers can read and respond to it early. Preprints are labeled as not yet peer-reviewed.
terms.does_not_mean: A preprint is not a published, vetted finding. Its numbers and conclusions may change — or the work may be withdrawn — after review, so it should be read with extra caution.

terms.plain_language: Compounding is when a pharmacy prepares a customized version of a medicine for an individual patient's prescription — for example, when a patient cannot use the standard manufactured form. Compounded preparations are not FDA-approved as finished products.
terms.does_not_mean: It does not mean a compounded preparation has passed the FDA approval process. This explainer states the regulatory fact only; it makes no claim about any compounded product's safety, quality, or effects.

terms.plain_language: "Investigational" describes a substance that researchers are studying but that no regulator has approved for any medical use. It may be tested in a laboratory, in animals, or — only inside regulated clinical trials — in people. The word names a status: being studied is not the same as being approved, available, or shown to work.
terms.does_not_mean: It does not mean the substance is safe, effective, legally available as a treatment, or likely to be approved. Most investigational substances never become approved medicines, and material sold outside regulated trials is not the product the researchers studied.

index_notes.tb_500: TB-500 is a laboratory fragment of the protein thymosin beta-4 — not the same substance. It has never been studied in humans, and it is not an approved medicine.
